claims.text: Adding approximately 2–3 at% Hf to nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 will suppress Cr–V-rich precipitate formation near 8 dpa.
Hf addition will form Hf-solute complexes in the W matrix.
Hf-solute complexes will lower the mobility of Cr and V.
Lower Cr and V mobility will reduce diffusion-driven clustering and nucleation of Cr–V-rich precipitates during irradiation.
The Hf-solute complexes will be uniformly distributed within the W matrix and bind Cr and V atoms.
Hf modification will preserve the alloy's low irradiation-induced hardening.
Hf modification will preserve the alloy's high radiation resistance.
The proposed mechanism will maintain the nanocrystalline structure during irradiation.
At approximately 8 dpa, the Hf-doped alloy will have a markedly lower density of Cr–V-rich precipitates than the unmodified alloy.
The Hf-doped alloy will retain a low ductile-brittle transition temperature.
Optimized processing will minimize unwanted Hf-rich secondary phases.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibits significant Cr–V-rich precipitate formation under irradiation near 8 dpa.
Cr–V-rich precipitate formation in unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11 increases irradiation hardening.
Cr–V-rich precipitate formation in unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11 raises the ductile-brittle transition temperature.
The hypothesis is applicable up to 8 dpa at specimen temperatures below 500°C.
Mechanical alloying followed by conventional consolidation such as hot isostatic pressing can provide a practically bulk-manufacturable Hf-modified alloy.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis characterizes the unmodified alloy as having low or negligible irradiation hardening that should be preserved, whereas the baseline says its Cr–V precipitates cause increased hardening. The baseline hardening state is therefore internally inconsistent.
